current_status: As of Nov 23, 2026 (America/Phoenix): the planned in-place detonation had not occurred. The original date was Nov 20; the Army postponed to Nov 23, then announced Nov 25. The Eighth Circuit issued an administrative stay of EPA's emergency treatment permit on Nov 19, pending a ruling on the emergency stay motion in No. 26-3374; as of a CourtListener docket review on Nov 23, that merits ruling had not issued. Iowa Public Radio reported that President Trump posted on Truth Social on Nov 23 that he ordered the military not to proceed until the Eighth Circuit agrees they can go forward, and subject to Gov.-elect Rob Sand agreeing. IAAAP also holds a regular RCRA OB/OD permit (EPA ID IA7213820445) listed as permitted through Sept 28, 2028. The emergency permit for in-place magazine detonation is a separate authorization, issued Nov 13, 2026, effective through Feb 11, 2027.
notes: The closest documented historical analog for bulk lead azide in deteriorating 55-gallon drums is Savanna Army Depot (1984). A March 21, 2014 Army article attributed DoD's 2004 green-primaries work to concern over a 40-year-old deteriorating lead azide stockpile at IAAAP. A separate research log kept with this draft has the claim-by-claim review.

current_status: A former Army depot. Official Army BRAC records recommend closing Savanna Army Depot Activity and relocating the U.S. Army Defense Ammunition Center and School to McAlester Army Ammunition Plant, Oklahoma. An Army BRAC NEPA public document states that SVADA ceased operations and officially closed on May 20, 2000. The depot was listed on the EPA National Priorities List on October 15, 1984. Parcel conveyance has continued; a DENIX page updated July 15, 2026, lists starting acreage of 12,884.32, conveyed 5,363.76, and remaining 7,520.56, with current owners including USFWS, USACE, Illinois DNR, and the Jo-Carroll Depot Local Redevelopment Authority. This draft still has not found an official document that accounts for the remaining bulk lead azide drums after the 1984 repack — including whether they were later destroyed, sold, or transferred (for example when the ammunition school moved to McAlester). A 1990 USADACS paper presented from Savanna discusses electrochemical reduction as a process demonstrated on lead azide, but it does not state the fate of the remaining 1984 stockpile.
notes: Closest documented historical analog to IAAAP's bulk lead azide drums. Depot closed May 20, 2000. The post-1984 fate of the remaining lead azide remains a research gap; no official destruction or transfer record for that residual stockpile was found in this pass.

name: Lone Star Army Ammunition Plant
known_energetics: An official Army BRAC installation report (updated November 3, 2025; compilation updated January 23, 2026) says Lone Star Army Ammunition Plant performed a load-assemble-pack munitions production mission for more than 60 years on 11 production lines. The 2005 BRAC Commission recommended relocating storage and demilitarization functions to McAlester AAP; 105mm and 155mm ICM artillery, MLRS artillery, hand grenades, and 60mm and 81mm mortars to Milan AAP; mines and detonators/relays/delays functions to Iowa AAP; and demolition-charges functions to Crane Army Ammunition Activity. That official relocation of detonator functions to IAAAP is not, by itself, a documented origin for IAAAP's 2026 lead azide drums. Day & Zimmermann–Lone Star remains the Army's agent for two RCRA-regulated units, the High Explosives Burning Ground and the High Explosives Demolition Ground. EPA lists this EPA ID (TXR000084774) separately from Day & Zimmermann Lone Star Facility (TXR000080174).
current_status: The same official BRAC report states that all active missions ceased and the plant closed as part of BRAC 2005 on September 30, 2009. A staff of two federal employees remain for caretaker oversight; caretaker operations are executed by Day & Zimmermann–Lone Star under a cost-plus caretaker contract. As of the November 3, 2025 update, 14,292 of 15,589 acres had been conveyed; 1,297 acres remained, with conveyance depending on cleanup. The site is on the National Priorities List. EPA's current OB/OD list still shows Lone Star Army Ammunition Plant as permitted, with a listed expiration of January 16, 2031.
notes: Closed production plant under BRAC caretaker and cleanup; remaining RCRA OB/OD units are in caretaker/agent status. This draft does not claim that IAAAP's 68 drums came from Lone Star.

name: Utah Test and Training Range
known_energetics: Utah RCRA permit Module III authorizes thermal treatment of hazardous-waste military munitions at UTTR in Box Elder County. Permitted wastes include unserviceable or serviceable excess munitions and explosive materials (examples in the module include bulk explosives, small-arms munitions, projectiles, flares, grenades, and sub-munitions) and unserviceable or serviceable excess solid-propellant components. The permittee may treat only hazardous-waste military munitions from allowed sources and is prohibited from treating hazardous waste from sources not authorized in the module. Treatment is described at Site 1 for open burning and Site 2 for open burning or open detonation. This draft does not have a current item-level inventory.
